title: The Fireworks AI Breach: How One Vendor Key Became a Supply Chain Attack on Cursor
content_md: TL;DR One read-only key started the chain: after Fireworks was breached, the attacker used a key provided by Cursor to copy agent traces. The credentials found in those traces gave access to Cursor’s internal tools. Up to 5,000 developers may have received a malicious extension: trojanized Claude Code builds sat in Cursor’s marketplace cache for about 11 hours on Oct. 29. The malicious builds were available between approximately 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Pacific time on October 29, 2026. Notion’s exposure was separate: chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of workspaces were exposed. Notion revoked exposed Notion API keys and notified the issuing providers about exposed third-party API keys. Where GitGuardian fits: Developer Endpoint Protection shows which credentials sit on developer machines, and AI Hooks keep new secrets out of supported coding assistants. On October 10, Fireworks AI disclosed unauthorized access to its systems. Over the following weeks, Cursor and Notion disclosed how the breach affected them, and Cursor took down a trojanized Claude Code extension from its marketplace. The attacker moved from Fireworks into Cursor’s systems by using credentials stored in places their owners thought were secure. Below is a step-by-step overview of the credential chain, what the malicious extension did, and recommended changes for sharing credentials with AI vendors and coding tools.
